# 3. Set up a project

Run the setup once per repository, new or existing:

```text
/agent-team:setup                  (Claude Code)
use the setup skill                (Codex, OpenCode)
```

It works on a branch, `chore/agent-team-setup`, shows every change before
making it, and ends with a commit you can review as a merge request.

## The steps

1. **Profile.** A few questions decide which parts of the template the
   project gets: tools, CI, issue tracker, roles, features (below).
2. **Install.** Only the files of the profile are copied. Existing files are
   never overwritten: the ones that differ are shown to you and merged with
   your approval.
3. **Interview.** Project name, stack, commands, folders per role, design
   system, models. If the repository already has code, the agent reads it
   first and turns what it finds into proposals you only confirm.
4. **Edits and checks.** The agent fills in the template with your answers
   and runs the checks: scripts, workflows, hooks, the tools' own validation.
5. **Skills.** It proposes skills for your stack (React, Postgres, GitHub
   Actions...) and installs them only after your yes, in a commit of their own.
6. **Project design.** A [design studio](04-run-the-project.md#design) session
   writes `docs/design/project.md`: goal, users, scope, roadmap by milestone.
   The setup is not finished without it.
7. **Foundations**, in a new repository: the spec of a walking skeleton
   (structure, contract, database, tests, green CI), the first task to build.
8. **Issues**, if you use a tracker: the roadmap becomes milestones and
   issues, after a dry run you approve.

## The profile

The profile says which parts of the template your project uses. It lives in
`.agent-team/config.json`:

```json
{
  "harnesses": ["claude", "codex"],
  "runners": {"optimizer": "codex"},
  "ci": "github",
  "tracker": "github",
  "roles": ["designer", "frontend", "backend", "devops", "optimizer", "security"],
  "features": ["ci-agents", "split", "dispatch"]
}
```

| Key | Values | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `harnesses` | `claude`, `codex`, `opencode` | the tools people and CI use; the first one leads and runs every role not listed in `runners` |
| `runners` | role → tool | roles that run on another tool, for example the optimizer on Codex |
| `ci` | `github`, `gitlab`, `both`, `none` | the CI platform of the project |
| `tracker` | `github`, `gitlab`, `local`, `jira`, `linear`, `redmine`, `none` | where the issues live ([4. Run the project](04-run-the-project.md#issues)) |
| `roles` | the six roles | drop the ones you do not need |
| `features` | `ci-agents`, `team-tasks`, `split`, `dispatch`, `litellm` | agents started from issues in CI; one issue run by several roles; split proposals in CI; start ready tasks at every merge; the LiteLLM gateway |

Every template file and section belongs to some part of the profile.
Whatever your profile does not use is removed during setup, so you customize
only what you use and no agent reads instructions for a tool you do not have.
Nothing is lost: change the profile later and the upgrade brings the files
back ([8. Change and upgrade](08-change-and-upgrade.md)).

**Which profile for which scenario:**

| Scenario | Typical profile |
|---|---|
| Local | your tool(s); `ci` for the project's CI; `tracker` `none` or `local`; no features |
| Remote repository | one or more tools; `ci` and `tracker` the same platform; `ci-agents`, plus `split`, `team-tasks`, `dispatch` as you like |
| Custom orchestrator | the tools your orchestrator runs; the tracker of its intake; a `start_command` ([7. Scenario: custom](07-scenario-custom.md)) |

## What you get

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `AGENTS.md` | rules for every agent and tool: boundaries, contract, alignment, merge requests, CI |
| `CLAUDE.md` | Claude Code only: imports `AGENTS.md`, plus a few Claude-specific notes |
| `docs/roles/*.md` | one prompt per role, shared by all tools |
| `docs/design/` | `project.md`, one spec per feature, templates |
| `docs/agents/` | rules by situation (workflow, alignment, merge requests, CI, splitting, team tasks) |
| `docs/alignment/` | one entry per change that other roles rely on |
| `docs/api/` | the API contract, owned by backend |
| `.claude/` | Claude Code: agents, settings with denied commands and hooks, skills |
| `.codex/` | Codex: settings, the role agents, hooks, forbidden commands |
| `.opencode/`, `opencode.json` | OpenCode: the role agents and their permissions |
| `.agents/skills/` | the project skills for Codex (and OpenCode without Claude Code) |
| `scripts/hooks/` | hooks shared by Claude Code and Codex: block commands on real environments, handoff notes, test gate |
| `.github/`, `.gitlab/`, `ci/` | the project CI and, for remote work, the agent workflows |
| `scripts/` | issues, split, dispatch, tracker check, profile |
| `.agent-team/` | the profile, and the record of the installed template that makes upgrades safe |

`SETUP.md` is the setup procedure; delete it when the setup is done.

## After the setup

- Read the open items the setup left you (secrets, labels, branch
  protection): they depend on the scenario.
- Build the foundations task first, then design the first feature with
  `/agent-team:design-studio <feature>`.
- Commit `.agent-team/`: upgrades need it.

# 4. Run the project

This chapter is the same in every scenario: how you design, plan, start,
review and keep the team aligned. The scenario chapters only add how agents
run and how a task starts.

## Design

Large decisions are made in a design studio session between you and the
designer, never in the middle of a task:

```text
/agent-team:design-studio login        (Claude Code, with the plugin)
/design-studio login                   (Claude Code or OpenCode, in the project)
use the design-studio skill for login  (Codex)
```

The designer asks in rounds of at most five numbered questions, each with a
recommended answer, so you can reply in one line ("1 yes, 2 yes, 3: option B").
Facts it can find in the repository, it looks up instead of asking. The rounds
go from goal and user flows to screens, data and API, **test seams** (the
interfaces the tests go through), the **task breakdown** and a readiness check.

The result is a spec, `docs/design/<feature>.md`, written as the session goes,
so you can stop and resume. It is marked `ready: yes` only when no question is
left open. Its task breakdown lists one row per task: role, what, dependencies.
The first session of a project writes `docs/design/project.md`, whose roadmap
lists the milestones (`M0`, `M1`...) and the features in each.

Agents implement only what a ready spec says: a task without one stops and
asks. Run the design studio again to revise a spec: past decisions are kept,
and rows that already have an issue are not rewritten.

## Issues

With a tracker, the roadmap and the ready specs become issues:

```text
/agent-team:create-issues       or      python3 scripts/create-issues.py --dry-run
                                         python3 scripts/create-issues.py
```

- one **milestone** per roadmap milestone (a version in Jira and Redmine, a
  project milestone in Linear);
- in it, one **issue per row** of every ready spec's breakdown, with the
  role, the spec, the acceptance criteria and the dependencies;
- one **"Design: <feature>"** issue for every feature that has no spec yet.

It shows the plan first and creates only on your yes. It adds no labels, so
nothing starts on its own. Running it again creates only what is missing, so
run it after every design session. With `--team`, a spec that allows it
becomes one team issue instead of one issue per task.

Supported trackers: GitHub, GitLab, Jira, Linear, Redmine, and plain Markdown
files in `docs/tasks/` for a project without a tracker. Check the connection
before the first run:

```bash
python3 scripts/tracker.py check     # which tracker, authenticated, readable; writes nothing
python3 scripts/tracker.py list      # open issues: role, milestone, dependencies, started or not
```

Credentials come from environment variables, never from files:
`JIRA_EMAIL` and `JIRA_API_TOKEN` (or `JIRA_PAT`), `LINEAR_API_KEY`,
`REDMINE_API_KEY`; `gh` or `glab` must be logged in for GitHub and GitLab.

## Split

An issue written by hand ("orders: filter by date") often needs several
roles. Splitting turns it into one task issue per role, as sub-issues in the
same milestone:

```text
/agent-team:split-issue 42
```

The agent reads the issue, the spec and the existing sub-issues, and proposes
a plan: a table of tasks with role, dependencies, acceptance criteria and the
folders each one touches. You change it in the conversation until it is right.
Only after your yes, the plan is posted on the issue and a script creates
exactly those issues: the model does not create anything itself. Running it
again creates nothing new.

### Several issues at once

Give several numbers, or a milestone (its open issues that have no sub-issues,
are not "Design:" issues and were not made by `create-issues`):

```text
/agent-team:split-issue 12 15 18
/agent-team:split-issue --milestone M1
```

The agent reads all of them first, with the specs and the existing sub-issues,
so the plans fit: no work twice, and the API contract is planned once. It
shows one overview: a table per issue (role, task, depends on), the
dependencies between issues, then numbered questions with a recommended
answer. You approve per issue, in one line:

```text
ok 12, 15; 18: merge the two frontend tasks
skip 21
```

Only what you asked is revised, and the overview is shown again until each
issue is approved or skipped. Then the issues are created in dependency order,
each one with its own proposal comment and its own `create`.

A task can wait for a task of another issue: `"depends_on": ["12:api"]` in the
plan means the task with key `api` of the plan of issue 12. It is written in
"Depends on" and as the tracker's native "blocked by" relation. If that task
does not exist yet, `create` refuses and creates nothing: split issue 12 first.
In CI (`agent:split`) each issue is still proposed and approved on its own.

In the remote scenario you can also split from the issue itself
([6. Scenario: remote](06-scenario-remote.md#split-from-the-issue)).

## Start

A task starts when its dependencies are merged. You can start tasks one by
one, or let dispatch pick the ready ones:

```text
/agent-team:dispatch        or      python3 scripts/dispatch.py           (the plan)
                                     python3 scripts/dispatch.py --apply   (start it)
```

Dispatch takes the first milestone that has open task issues, counts what is
running, and starts the tasks whose dependencies are all closed as completed:
by default one per role and three in total (`--per-role`, `--max`). It never
starts optimizer or security, "Design:" issues, or issues marked `hold`.

"Design:" issues and issues without a role are not tasks yet. Under "Not tasks
yet" the plan lists how many are open in that milestone and the earlier ones,
with the command that turns them into tasks (`design-studio` then
`create-issues`, or `split-issue`). So if dispatch works on M2 while M0 still
has "Design:" issues, the plan says so.

What "start" means depends on the scenario: a label that starts a CI job, a
GitLab pipeline, a command of your orchestrator, or a printed instruction for
a local session. That is the *starter* ([9. Reference](09-reference.md#starters)).

## Review and merge

Every merge request describes itself in the same sections:

- **Summary**: what changed and why.
- **Evidence**: before and after; screenshots for UI changes.
- **Merge danger**: can it simply be reverted, or does it migrate data or
  break a client; who feels it.
- **Not done**: what the agent decided not to do.
- **Reviewer checks**: what to look at.
- **Alignment impact**: the alignment entry, or "none".

The CI checks every merge request the same way, yours or an agent's: build,
type check, tests, UI screenshots per viewport (once you turn on the UI tests), static analysis (only the
findings the change introduces fail it), licenses, vulnerabilities, secrets.
Turn on branch protection so `main` only moves through merge requests that
are up to date and green.

You merge. Closing the issue frees the role's slot and its dependents can start.

## Alignment

When an agent changes something other roles rely on (the API contract, the
data model, a shared component, a route, an environment variable), it does not
fix their code. It writes an entry in `docs/alignment/` and flags the merge
request with an "Alignment impact" section and, in CI, the `alignment-needed`
label.

- **In a local session** the lead handles it right away: designer reviews the
  change against the specs and writes the follow-up per role, the lead
  delegates them, the entry is closed. You are asked only when designer marks
  a decision as yours (a breaking API change, a visible UX change).
- **In CI** agents never start other agents. The label is your signal: create
  the follow-up tasks, designer first.

Breaking contract changes are planned as expand-contract: add the new form,
move the callers, remove the old form last, with `main` green at every step.

## Team tasks

A small, tightly coupled feature can be one task for several roles: one
issue, one branch, one merge request. A coordinator runs the roles in order,
each one committing before the next starts. Use it when separate merge
requests would only wait on each other; prefer separate tasks otherwise.
Team tasks need the `team-tasks` feature and, in CI, Claude Code.

## On-demand roles

- **optimizer**: "use optimizer on the orders list" when a measurement shows a
  problem. It works only with green tests, and shows timings before and after.
- **security**: "run a security assessment" once the app runs, typically
  before a release. It attacks only the hosts listed in
  `docs/roles/security-scope.txt` (local or staging, never production) and
  writes a report in `docs/security/`, kept out of Git. The owning roles fix
  the findings as separate tasks.

## Long sessions

Claude Code and Codex sessions are compacted at 200,000 tokens instead of near the model's limit:
every turn re-reads the whole context, so a long session costs more and
forgets distant instructions. When a session has grown long or changes phase
(design to implementation, one task to the next), ask for a **handoff**:
`/handoff` in Claude Code and OpenCode, the handoff skill in Codex. It writes
a short note in `.handoff/`; start a new session and it continues from the
note with a small context.

# 5. Scenario: local

The team runs on your computer, inside your session. You talk to a lead
session, which delegates to the role agents and reports back. Everything in
[4. Run the project](04-run-the-project.md) applies; this chapter adds how to
work with each tool.

## Why use it

| Good for | Watch out |
|---|---|
| Starting in minutes: no secrets, no workflows, no server | You need to be there: when you close the session, the work stops |
| A tight feedback loop: you see each step and correct it at once | One machine: tasks run one after another or a few at a time, on your laptop's resources |
| Exploring, prototypes, small features, design work | Less trail: decisions live in commits and specs, not in issue threads, unless you also use a tracker |
| Alignment handled automatically: the lead runs designer and the affected roles right away | Your subscription or API budget pays for every turn of every agent |
| Your own credentials and tools, no CI minutes | Long sessions grow expensive: use handoff notes |

Choose it to begin with, for one-person projects, and for the design work of
any project. Move to the [remote scenario](06-scenario-remote.md) when the
backlog grows and you want the team to work while you do something else.

## Profile

```json
{"harnesses": ["claude"], "ci": "github", "tracker": "none", "features": []}
```

Use `"tracker": "local"` to keep issues as Markdown files in `docs/tasks/`,
or your real tracker if the project has one: issues, splits and dispatch work
the same. Keep `ci` for the project's own CI: it checks your merge requests
even when nobody runs agents there.

## With Claude Code

Start `claude` in the repository. The roles are subagents in `.claude/agents/`:

```text
> @backend implement task 2 of docs/design/login.md
> implement the login feature from docs/design/login.md   (the lead delegates by role)
> @devops add a staging deploy job                       (it writes the config, never applies it)
```

- Each agent preloads its skills and has its own context; the lead receives a
  summary, not the whole work.
- Hooks: commands that change real environments are blocked for everyone; a
  task cannot be closed while the tests fail; after each delegation the lead
  is reminded of open alignment entries; frontend files are linted when saved.
- Denied commands (`git push --force`, push to `main`, merge, `terraform
  apply`...) are in `.claude/settings.json`.
- **Agent teams** (experimental in Claude Code): several agents work in
  parallel and message each other. Turn them on with
  `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS` set to `"1"` in `.claude/settings.json`.
  Good for a feature where frontend and backend must agree as they go.

## With Codex

Start `codex` in the repository and trust it when asked: only then Codex
reads `.codex/`. Approve the project hooks once with `/hooks`.

```text
> have backend implement task 2 of docs/design/login.md
> spawn frontend and backend in parallel for docs/design/login.md, tasks 2 and 3
```

- The roles are custom agents in `.codex/agents/*.toml`, each with its
  reasoning effort; at most three run at once.
- Forbidden commands are in `.codex/rules/agent-team.rules`, and the same
  hook as Claude Code blocks commands on real environments.
- Codex has no per-agent hooks: the test gate and the alignment reminder are
  rules in `AGENTS.md` that the lead follows, not checks.
- Pin the model in `.codex/config.toml` if you do not want Codex's default.

## With OpenCode

Start `opencode` in the repository. The roles are agents in
`.opencode/agents/`, usable as subagents (`@backend ...`) or as the main agent
(switch with Tab).

- Permissions are rules in `opencode.json` and in each agent: commands on
  real environments and merges are denied, other shell commands ask first.
- OpenCode has no hooks in the template: its permission rules are the
  protection.
- With LiteLLM (feature `litellm`) OpenCode reaches any provider through one
  gateway with budgets per key ([7. Scenario: custom](07-scenario-custom.md#litellm-one-gateway-for-many-providers)).

## Several tools in one project

People in the same project can use different tools: list them all in
`harnesses`. They share `AGENTS.md`, the role prompts, the specs and the
skills; each tool reads its own folder. The design, the issues and the
handoff notes are the same for everybody.

## Issues in the local scenario

A local session does not need issues: give the lead a spec and a task number.
With a tracker, the lead can pick work from it:

```text
> python3 scripts/dispatch.py      shows the ready tasks
> implement issue #14              the lead reads it and delegates to its role
```

The default starter for trackers other than GitHub and GitLab prints the
command to start each task; with `"starter": "command"` it can open a new
terminal session for you instead ([9. Reference](09-reference.md#starters)).

## The skills by example

A short example of each skill in a local project (profile with `"tracker":
"local"`, issues as files in `docs/tasks/`). Replies are in one line: the
agent asks numbered questions and you answer by number.

**setup** - once, in an empty or existing repository:

```text
> /agent-team:setup
  (it asks harnesses, tracker, roles, stack; "1 claude, 2 local, 3 all roles")
```

**next** - when you do not know what to do:

```text
> /agent-team:next
  Design: project ready, "login" ready, "orders" not. Issues: none yet.
  Next: /agent-team:create-issues
```

**design-studio** - before building a feature:

```text
> /agent-team:design-studio orders
  Round 1 - 1. Who filters the list? (recommended: the customer) ...
> 1 yes, 2 by date and status, 3: option B
```

**create-issues** - after a design session; it shows the plan first:

```text
> /agent-team:create-issues
  milestone create   M0 · Walking skeleton
  issue create       Login · 1/3 · backend: Auth endpoint ...
> yes
```

**split-issue** - for an issue written by hand, in `docs/tasks/`:

```text
> /agent-team:split-issue 7
  1 backend: date filter in the API   2 frontend: date picker (after 1)
> ok 7
```

**dispatch** - to see what is ready; in a local project the starter prints the
command to run in a new session:

```text
> /agent-team:dispatch
  Would start (2): #1 backend, #3 devops. Waits: #2 (needs #1)
> yes
```

**upgrade** - after a new plugin version, or to add a tool:

```text
> /agent-team:upgrade
  update 3 files, merge 1, add 2. Work on a branch, one commit.
> yes
```

## From your phone

To drive the session from the Claude app, start it with Remote Control:

```bash
claude --remote-control "my-project"     # or type /remote-control in a session
```

Then open the session in the app and ask "what's next?" (Claude runs `next`) or
type `/agent-team:dispatch`. The terminal must stay running: the work happens
on your computer, the app is only a window on it.

# 6. Scenario: remote repository

The team works in your GitHub or GitLab CI. A task is an issue; you start it
with a label (GitHub) or a pipeline (GitLab); the agent runs in a job, pushes
a branch and opens a merge request. You come back to review and merge.
Everything in [4. Run the project](04-run-the-project.md) applies.

## Why use it

| Good for | Watch out |
|---|---|
| You do not need to be there: start tasks, close the laptop, review the merge requests later | Slower feedback: a mistake shows up in the merge request, not while it happens |
| Several tasks in parallel, each in a clean environment | Every run costs tokens (or subscription quota) and CI minutes |
| A full trail: issue, plan comment, branch, merge request, CI results | An hour of set-up: secrets, labels, branch protection, required checks |
| The whole team (people too) sees the same board: issues, milestones, merge requests | Agents in CI never start other agents: alignment follow-ups are yours to create |
| Merges can start the next tasks automatically | Untrusted text: issues are read as task descriptions, and only members can start agents |
| Several tools in one project, chosen per role | A Codex or OpenCode job on GitLab is not yet proven on real runners: try it on a test task |

Choose it once the project has a backlog, when you want work to continue
while you are away, or when several people review the team's work.

## Profile

```json
{"harnesses": ["claude"], "ci": "github", "tracker": "github",
 "features": ["ci-agents", "split", "team-tasks", "dispatch"]}
```

With several tools, list them and assign roles to the others:
`"harnesses": ["claude", "codex"], "runners": {"optimizer": "codex"}`.

## GitHub

### Set up once

1. **Secrets** (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions), for the tools
   in your profile:

   | Tool | Secrets | Variables |
   |---|---|---|
   | Claude Code | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` for a subscription (`claude setup-token`) | |
   | Codex | `OPENAI_API_KEY`; `AGENT_PR_TOKEN` (optional, see below) | `CODEX_MODEL` (optional) |
   | OpenCode | the keys of your providers, or the LiteLLM key | `OPENCODE_MODEL` (`provider/model`) |

   For Claude Code, also install the GitHub app: `/install-github-app` in a
   Claude Code session. With a subscription token, switch the workflows from
   `anthropic_api_key` to `claude_code_oauth_token`.
2. **Labels**: `./scripts/create-labels.sh` creates `agent:<role>` for your
   roles, `agent:team`, `agent:split`, `hold`, `alignment-needed`, `ai-review`.
3. **Branch protection** on `main`: pull requests only, the CI checks
   required, "Require branches to be up to date before merging".
4. **Routing**, with more than one tool: the `AGENT_RUNNERS` repository
   variable says which role runs where, for example
   `{"agent:frontend":"opencode","agent:optimizer":"codex"}`. The other roles
   run on the first tool of the profile (`AGENT_DEFAULT_RUNNER` changes it).

### Start a task

Add the label `agent:<role>` to a task issue (or run dispatch, which adds
them for you). The workflow `agents.yml` starts the agent of that role:

- **Claude Code**: the agent comments its plan on the issue, works on a
  branch, runs the tests, opens the pull request and comments its link.
- **Codex**: runs without network or tokens on a checkout with the
  dependencies installed; a second job commits its change, pushes the branch
  and opens the pull request with Codex's summary as the description. Pull
  requests opened with the default token do not trigger other workflows: set
  `AGENT_PR_TOKEN` (a fine-grained token with contents and pull requests
  write) so the CI checks them.
- **OpenCode**: its GitHub action runs the role agent and opens the pull request.

Only issues opened by the owner, members, collaborators or the repository's
own workflows can start agents. The issue text is read as a description of
the task, never as instructions that override the project rules.

### Start the next tasks at every merge

`dispatch.yml` runs dispatch every time an issue closes, so the tasks that
were waiting start as soon as you merge what they depend on. It is off until
you set the variable `AGENT_AUTODISPATCH` to `true` and the secret
`AGENT_DISPATCH_TOKEN` (a fine-grained token with issues read and write:
labels added with the default token do not start other workflows). Limits:
`AGENT_DISPATCH_PER_ROLE` (default 1) and `AGENT_DISPATCH_MAX` (default 3).
Keep them low at first: every start is an agent run.

### Split from the issue

Add `agent:split` to an issue. Claude reads it with the specs and posts a
proposed split as a comment; nothing is created. Then reply on the issue:

| Reply | Result |
|---|---|
| `@claude ok` | the proposed issues are created as sub-issues, without labels |
| `@claude ok team` | one team issue instead, when the proposal suggests it |
| `@claude <your changes>` | a new proposal |

A script creates exactly the plan you approved; the model creates nothing.

### Team tasks

Add `agent:team` to an issue with a line `Roles: backend, frontend`. A
coordinator runs the listed roles in order on one branch and opens one pull
request with a section per role. Needs Claude Code.

### Ask and review

- `@claude <request>` in a comment on an issue or a pull request: Claude
  answers or makes the change on that branch.
- Label a pull request `ai-review` for two reviews in parallel: one against
  the project's rules (inline comments), one against the issue and the spec.
  They never approve or block. Remove and re-add the label to review again.

Mentions, reviews, splits and team tasks use Claude Code. With only Codex or
OpenCode, split locally with `/agent-team:split-issue` and review in your tool.

## GitLab

Agents run as jobs of `.gitlab/ci/agents.yml`, included by `.gitlab-ci.yml`
(rename the template's `.gitlab-ci.yml.example`). They start only when you
run a pipeline with variables, never on pushes:

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `AI_FLOW_INPUT` | the task, or "carry out issue 14 following docs/roles/backend.md" |
| `TASK_ID` | the issue number: jobs for the same task queue instead of running together |
| `AI_FLOW_ROLE` | the role (needed by Codex and OpenCode) |
| `AI_FLOW_HARNESS` | `claude`, `codex` or `opencode`; default: the first tool of the profile |
| `AI_FLOW_ROLES` | a team task: the roles in order, for example `backend, frontend` |
| `SPLIT_ISSUE`, `SPLIT_CONFIRM`, `SPLIT_FEEDBACK` | the split: proposal, then `ok` or `team` |

Run them from CI/CD → Pipelines → Run pipeline, or let dispatch do it: on
GitLab its starter adds the label and runs the pipeline with these variables.

Masked variables: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (or the subscription token),
`OPENAI_API_KEY` for Codex, the provider keys and `OPENCODE_MODEL` for
OpenCode, and `GITLAB_ACCESS_TOKEN` (a project access token with `api` and
`write_repository`) for splits and for the Codex and OpenCode jobs, which
push and open the merge request after the agent has finished. Protect `main`
and require the pipeline to pass before merging. GitLab reads the code owners
from `.gitlab/CODEOWNERS`.

## Costs and safety

- Each task is one agent run; a team task is several. The CI minutes are
  those of your plan.
- Agents in CI use `--max-turns` limits, compact at 200,000 tokens and never
  run in the background, so a run ends with a merge request or a comment
  saying why it could not.
- Agents never merge, never push to `main`, never apply infrastructure. The
  CI checks their merge requests like anyone else's, and the actions in the
  workflows are pinned to commits, with Dependabot proposing updates.

# 7. Scenario: custom orchestrator

Here the issues live in the tracker you already use, and the agents run where
you decide, started by something you control. Agent team gives you the
planning side (design, issues, split, dispatch) on any supported tracker, and
one hook for the execution side: the *starter command*. What runs the agents
is up to you; this chapter shows two ways.

Everything in [4. Run the project](04-run-the-project.md) applies.

## Why use it

| Good for | Watch out |
|---|---|
| Your tracker: Jira, Linear, Redmine, or GitHub/GitLab issues with your own runner | You build and run the execution side: a service, a server, its updates |
| Your infrastructure: the code never leaves your network, your runners, your credentials | Protections are yours too: tokens that cannot push to `main` or merge, no production credentials where agents run |
| Control: priorities, queues, retries, concurrency, cost per task, any mix of tools and models | More moving parts to watch than a CI job |
| A board people already use, with agents as one more kind of assignee | The CI workflows in the template are for GitHub and GitLab: on other platforms, keep your own CI |

Choose it when the first two scenarios are not enough for a concrete reason:
a company tracker, code that must stay on your machines, a queue with
priorities. Otherwise start [remote](06-scenario-remote.md) and move later.

## The connection points

**Planning, on your tracker.** Set it in the profile and check it:

```json
{
  "harnesses": ["claude", "opencode"],
  "ci": "none",
  "tracker": "jira",
  "jira": {"url": "https://example.atlassian.net", "project": "APP"},
  "starter": "command",
  "start_command": "python3 /opt/team/enqueue.py --issue {number} --role {role} --harness {harness} --url {url}"
}
```

```bash
python3 scripts/tracker.py check
```

| Concept | Jira | Linear | Redmine | Files (`local`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Milestone | version (Fix Version) | project milestone | version | `docs/tasks/_milestones.json` |
| Sub-issue | sub-task | sub-issue | parent task | `parent` field |
| Dependency | "Blocks" link | "blocks" relation | "blocks" relation | text |
| Started | label `agent:<role>` | label | status (`started_status`) | label |

Create issues, split and dispatch work as in chapter 4. The split proposal is
approved in your session instead of with a comment.

**Execution, through the starter.** When dispatch starts a task, it marks it
as started and runs `start_command` with the issue's data: `{number}` (12,
APP-12), `{id}`, `{ref}`, `{role}`, `{title}`, `{url}`, `{tracker}` and
`{harness}` (the tool for that role: `runners`, otherwise the first of the
profile). The command is split into arguments before the values are filled
in and runs without a shell, so an issue title cannot inject commands. A
command that fails is reported for that task (which stays marked as started:
remove the label to retry) and dispatch exits with an error.

So your orchestrator needs one entry point that accepts a task, and a way to
tell the tracker when the work is done (a merge request linked to the issue,
or a status change). Two ways to build the rest follow.

## Option A: Multica, a board with agents as team members

[Multica](https://github.com/multica-ai/multica) is a self-hosted board where
agents appear as team members: you assign an issue to an agent as to a
colleague, it picks up the work, updates the status and reports blockers. A
daemon on a server of yours runs the installed tools (Claude Code, Codex,
OpenCode and others).

How it fits:

- One agent per role in Multica, each with its tool (runtime) and model.
  Point them to the role prompts: "follow docs/roles/<role>.md and AGENTS.md".
- Plan with Agent team (design studio, specs), then create and assign the
  tasks in Multica, by hand or from `start_command` through its API.
- A server with at least 4 vCPUs and 8 GB of RAM (builds and tests run
  there), the tools installed and logged in as the daemon's user, a Git token
  that can open merge requests but never push to `main` or merge, and no
  cluster, cloud or registry credentials on that machine.

Good when you want a visual board for agents running on different tools.
Multica is young and changes fast: check its README before installing.

## Option B: your own orchestrator

A small service that takes tasks from a queue and runs the right tool in a
clean checkout. The starter command only enqueues; a worker does the rest:

```text
dispatch.py --apply  →  start_command (enqueue)  →  queue  →  worker
                                                      worker: checkout, run the tool, push, open the MR,
                                                              update the tracker with the result and the cost
```

The worker runs each tool non-interactively, in the repository, with the
same prompt the CI jobs use:

| Tool | Command |
|---|---|
| Claude Code | `claude -p "<task>" --permission-mode acceptEdits --max-turns 40` |
| Codex | `codex exec --sandbox workspace-write --output-last-message summary.md "<task>"` |
| OpenCode | `opencode run --agent <role> --model <provider/model> "<task>"` |

For more control, use the tools' libraries instead of their command lines:
the Claude Agent SDK (`@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` or `claude-agent-sdk`
for Python) streams each step and reports the cost of the run; load the
project settings (`settingSources: ["project"]`) so it reads `CLAUDE.md` and
`.claude/`.

Rules for the worker:

- one container or VM per task, with write access to that repository only;
- a Git token that can push branches and open merge requests, never push to
  `main` or merge;
- no production, cluster or registry credentials;
- record the cost and the outcome on the task, so you notice a role that
  burns budget.

Good when you need priorities, retries, your own infrastructure or a
dashboard of your own. It is your code to maintain: start with the simplest
queue that works.

## LiteLLM: one gateway for many providers

With OpenCode on several providers, the `litellm` feature adds
`infra/litellm/`: a LiteLLM gateway (with Postgres and Caddy) that gives each
role a virtual key with its own budget, and one place to see costs per role
and model. Run it next to your orchestrator, listening only on the local
interface, or on a small server for CI. `infra/litellm/key-spend.sh` shows
what each key spent; `docker-compose.local.yml` runs it on your computer for
a trial.

# 8. Change and upgrade

Two things change over a project's life: the plugin gets new versions, and
your setup changes (another tracker, Codex next to Claude Code, a role back,
the move from local to remote). Both go through the same command:

```text
/agent-team:upgrade        (Claude Code)
use the upgrade skill      (Codex, OpenCode)
```

## Change the profile

Tell the upgrade what changes ("move the issues to Linear", "add Codex for
the optimizer", "we no longer need the designer") or edit
`.agent-team/config.json` yourself, then run the upgrade. It renders the
template for the new profile and shows a plan:

| Kind | What happens |
|---|---|
| `add` | a file the new profile includes: added |
| `update` | a template file you never changed: replaced with the new version |
| `merge` | changed by both you and the template: three-way merge that keeps your changes |
| `prune` | a file the profile no longer includes, never changed by you: removed |
| `out-of-profile` | a file the profile no longer includes, changed by you: kept, you decide |
| `removed-by-you` | a file you deleted: not added back |

Sections follow the same rule: drop team tasks and their section leaves
`AGENTS.md`; add Codex back and its lines return, merged with your edits.
Conflicts, if any, are left marked and resolved with you. The upgrade works
on a branch and ends with a commit for you to review.

Examples:

| You want | Profile change | What the upgrade does |
|---|---|---|
| From local to remote on GitHub | `"tracker": "github"`, `"features": ["ci-agents", "dispatch"]` | adds the agent workflows, labels script, issue scripts; then the remote set-up of [chapter 6](06-scenario-remote.md#set-up-once) |
| Codex instead of Claude Code | `"harnesses": ["codex"]` | adds `.codex/` and `.agents/skills/`, removes `.claude/` and `CLAUDE.md` if unchanged, switches the CI jobs |
| Jira instead of GitHub issues | `"tracker": "jira"` plus its settings | adds the Jira adapter, removes the GitHub workflows that need GitHub issues |
| Security back | add `"security"` to `roles` | adds its prompt, agents and scope file |

After a tool change, the upgrade lists what that tool needs once: trust and
hooks for Codex, new CI secrets and variables.

Without the plugin, `python3 scripts/agent-team.py prune` removes what left
the profile, but only the upgrade can add things back.

## Upgrade to a new plugin version

1. Update the plugin ([2. Install](02-install.md#updating-the-plugin)).
2. Run `/agent-team:upgrade` in the project. It reads the release notes of
   the versions in between and explains each change, not just the file names.
3. Review the plan, exclude what you do not want, apply.
4. Do the steps listed in the release notes' "Upgrade notes": they are the
   ones a file change cannot do (new secrets, labels, required checks).

Every project stays on the template version it installed until you upgrade
it: updating the plugin changes nothing by itself.

## How your changes are kept

The setup stores a copy of every installed template file in
`.agent-team/base/`. The upgrade compares three versions of each file: that
copy, your file, and the new template file. If only the template changed,
your file is replaced; if only you changed it, nothing happens; if both
changed, `git merge-file` merges them and marks the lines it cannot decide.

`README.md`, `docs/design-decisions.md`, `.mcp.json` and
`docs/roles/security-scope.txt` are yours after setup: they are never upgraded.

## A project set up by hand

A project copied from the template without the plugin, or set up before the
plugin existed, has no `.agent-team/base/`. The first upgrade proposes a
profile from what the project has, then compares each file that differs with
you and records the result; later upgrades are automatic. Without Claude
Code, run it from a clone:

```bash
python3 ~/agent-team/scripts/template_sync.py status --template ~/agent-team/template --project .
python3 ~/agent-team/scripts/template_sync.py apply  --template ~/agent-team/template --project .
```

## Token costs

What every agent reads on every turn costs on every request: `AGENTS.md`
(about 1,200 tokens after setup), `CLAUDE.md`, the descriptions of the agents
and skills of the tool in use, and the tools of active MCP servers. Role
prompts, specs and `docs/agents/` cost only when an agent opens them. Files
of other tools, trackers and workflows cost nothing unless an agent searches
or opens them: the profile removes them anyway, so no agent stumbles on
instructions for tools you do not have.

To keep costs down: one task per session, handoff notes instead of long
sessions, MCP servers only on the agents that need them, and few skills per
role.

## This manual

The manual is written in Markdown, one file per chapter in `docs/manual/`.
`docs/manual.html` is generated from those files and never edited by hand:

```bash
pip install markdown==3.11.2
python3 scripts/build_manual.py           # regenerate docs/manual.html
python3 scripts/build_manual.py --check   # fails if the HTML is not built from the current Markdown
```

The HTML records a hash of the Markdown it was built from; `--check` compares
it with the files, and the repository's CI runs it on every pull request. To
check before every commit: `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`.

# Alignment changes

A change is an alignment change when another role relies on what you
changed: the API contract, the data model, a shared component or design
token, a route or user flow, an environment variable or port, the deployment
interface.

When you make one:
1. Copy `docs/alignment/_template.md` to
   `docs/alignment/<yyyy-mm-dd>-<task-id>.md` and fill it in, with
   `status: open`. One file per change, so parallel branches never conflict.
2. In the MR description add an `## Alignment impact` section that links the
   entry (write "none" when there is none). In CI also add the
   `alignment-needed` label to the MR.
3. Do not adapt other roles' code yourself.

What happens next depends on where you run:
- **Local session (Claude Code with subagents or agent teams):** the lead
  handles it right away. First designer reviews the change against the specs,
  updates `docs/design/` if needed and writes the follow-up actions per role
  in the entry. Then the lead delegates each action to its role. Finally the
  entry gets `status: resolved` and a short resolution. The lead stops and asks
  the user only when designer sets `decision-needed: yes` (for example a
  breaking API change or a visible UX change).
- **CI (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Multica):** agents never start other
  agents, except the coordinator of a team task (below). The entry and the
  label are the signal: the user reviews them and creates the alignment
  tasks, designer first, then the affected roles.

# CI

Every MR runs the project CI: build, type check, test, static analysis,
SBOM and license report, license policy, vulnerabilities, secrets and
misconfigurations (`ci/scan.sh`).
- A red CI is part of your task: fix the cause, never weaken the check. Do not
  edit `ci/scanners.env`, skip a test or add an ignore rule without the user's
  explicit approval in the MR.
- Static analysis: semgrep fails the MR on the findings your change
  introduces (details in `semgrep.txt`, artifact `static-analysis`). Fix the
  code. If you think a finding is a false positive, do not suppress it
  yourself: explain it in the MR under `## Static analysis` and let the user
  decide. A `nosemgrep: <rule-id>` comment, with the reason next to it, only
  with the user's approval.
- Workflow files: after editing anything in `.github/workflows/`, run
  `actionlint` (the `Workflow lint` check runs it on every PR). A job-level `if`
  can use only the `github`, `needs`, `vars`, `inputs` and `matrix` contexts:
  `hashFiles()` works in steps only, and one in a job `if` makes GitHub reject
  the whole file, so no job runs.
- UI tests: when `playwright.config.ts` exists, the `ui` job runs the tests
  in `e2e/` and keeps the report and the screenshots per viewport (artifact
  `ui-report`). A screen or state without its UI test is not done.
- When you run outside CI (a local session, the Multica daemon, the
  orchestrator), wait for the checks after opening the MR (`gh pr checks
  --watch`, or `glab ci status` until the pipeline ends), fix what fails and
  push again. Agents that run inside CI jobs do not wait: the user or the
  orchestrator sends the failures back.

# Branches and merge requests

- One branch per task, named `feat/<task-id>-<slug>` (in GitHub Actions, the
  branch the action creates for you).
- Before opening the MR, bring your branch up to date with `main` and run the
  tests again. Where you are not allowed to rebase (the Claude GitHub action),
  say in the MR that the branch must be updated before merging.
- Before opening the MR, check whether `main` changed the API contract or
  `docs/alignment/` since you started; if it did, adapt or report it.

## Merge request description
Every MR description has these sections, short:
- **Summary**: what changed and why; for a structural change, the smallest
  sketch that makes it clear (a call tree, a file tree, a diff of a component
  tree).
- **Evidence**: before and after. Screenshots for UI changes (the `ui-report`
  artifact, or `reports/ui/` locally), otherwise the test that failed before
  and passes now, or the command output.
- **Merge danger**: one-way or two-way door (can the merge simply be
  reverted, or does it migrate data, delete something, break a client?) and
  the blast radius in a few words (which users, screens or clients feel it).
- **Not done**: what you decided not to do, and why.
- **Reviewer checks**: what the reviewer must look at.
- **Alignment impact**: the `docs/alignment/` entry, or "none".

# Splitting issues

In CI the user can ask for a proposal that splits one issue into task issues,
one per role: the `agent:split` label on GitHub, `SPLIT_ISSUE` on GitLab. The
proposal is a plan in the format at the top of `scripts/agentteam/plans.py`; the
user approves it (`@claude ok`) and the script creates exactly that. Rules for
the plan:
- One task per role and per boundary (see "How work is delegated"): a task
  never makes two roles edit the same files.
- Follow the standard feature sequence: the API contract first when the
  feature changes it, then backend and frontend against it; devops only if
  the pipeline, the image or the manifests change.
- No ready spec for the work: propose a single designer task that writes it,
  or say in a comment that a design studio session with the user is needed.
  Never plan implementation tasks on missing design.
- A breaking contract change is planned as expand-contract (see "API
  contract"): the expand task, the tasks that move the callers (depending on
  it), a last contract task (depending on all of them).
- optimizer and security only when the issue asks for them explicitly.
- At most 6 tasks. If more are needed, say so and propose splitting the issue
  into features first.
- Every task has acceptance criteria someone can check without reading the
  code, and lists the files or folders it touches.
- Suggest a team task (`team` in the plan) when the work is small and tightly
  coupled (see "Team tasks").
- Never add labels: the user starts each task.

# Team tasks

A team task is one issue carried out by several roles in sequence on the same
branch, ending in one MR. The user asks for it explicitly: the `agent:team`
label on GitHub (with a `Roles: backend, frontend` line in the issue body),
`AI_FLOW_ROLES` on GitLab, or a request in a local session.
- A coordinator delegates only to the listed roles, in the listed order, and
  writes no code itself.
- Each role works within its own boundaries and commits and pushes before the
  next one starts.
- Alignment entries that concern listed roles are handled inside the task;
  the others stay open and are reported in the MR.
- Use team tasks for small, tightly coupled features. Larger work stays split
  into separate tasks, so that each MR remains reviewable.

# Standard feature sequence

1. designer writes the spec in `docs/design/`
2. backend updates the API contract, if the feature changes it
3. backend and frontend implement in parallel, against that contract
4. designer reviews the implementation
5. frontend applies the feedback
6. devops updates pipeline, image and manifests if the feature needs it
7. the MR is opened

Not every feature involves every role. A style change does not need
devops; an infrastructure migration does not need the designer. Involve
only the roles the task actually touches.

# Issue trackers and starters

The scripts that create, split and start tasks (`scripts/create-issues.py`,
`scripts/split-issue.py`, `scripts/dispatch.py`) talk to the tracker only
through `scripts/agentteam/core.py`: one interface, one adapter per tracker in
`scripts/agentteam/trackers/`. Python standard library only, nothing to install.

How a task is *started* is kept apart, on purpose: that part depends on your
setup (a label that triggers a workflow, a pipeline, an orchestrator). It is the
*starter*, in `scripts/agentteam/starters.py`.

## Trackers

| Tracker | Milestones | Sub-issues | Dependencies | Labels | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `github` | milestones | sub-issues | "blocked by" | yes | `gh` authenticated |
| `gitlab` | milestones | linked issues | "blocked by" links (Premium), otherwise text | yes | `glab` authenticated |
| `local` | `docs/tasks/_milestones.json` | `parent` field | text | yes | nothing: Markdown files in `docs/tasks/` |
| `jira` | versions (Fix Version) | sub-tasks | "Blocks" links | yes | `JIRA_EMAIL` + `JIRA_API_TOKEN` (Cloud) or `JIRA_PAT` (Data Center) |
| `linear` | project milestones | sub-issues | "blocks" relations | yes | `LINEAR_API_KEY` |
| `redmine` | versions | parent task | "blocks" relations | no: statuses instead | `REDMINE_API_KEY` |

Dependencies are always written in the issue text too ("Depends on"), so
`dispatch.py` works even where the tracker has no relation for them. On Jira,
Linear and Redmine the hidden markers the scripts use to recognize their issues
are a last plain line `[agent-team] ...` instead of an HTML comment; leave it.

## Starters

| Starter | What it does | Default on |
|---|---|---|
| `label` | adds `agent:<role>`; on GitHub that starts `.github/workflows/agents.yml` | GitHub |
| `gitlab-pipeline` | adds `agent:<role>` and runs the agent pipeline for the issue | GitLab |
| `command` | marks the task, then runs `start_command` with the issue's data | any, when `start_command` is set |
| `print` | marks the task and prints how to start it by hand | the other trackers |

`command` is the connector for a custom orchestrator: a queue, a
service, a local `claude -p`. Placeholders: `{number}` (12, PROJ-12), `{id}`
(#12), `{ref}`, `{role}`, `{title}`, `{url}`, `{tracker}`. The command is split
into arguments first and runs without a shell, so an issue title cannot inject
commands. A non-zero exit stops the dispatch.

## Configuration

`.agent-team/config.json`, all keys optional (`"auto"`: GitHub or GitLab from
the CI or the Git remote, `local` without a remote):

```json
{
  "tracker": "jira",
  "starter": "command",
  "start_command": "orchestrator enqueue --issue {number} --role {role}",
  "jira": {"url": "https://example.atlassian.net", "project": "APP"}
}
```

Other sections: `"linear": {"team": "ENG", "project": "App"}` (milestones need
a project), `"redmine": {"url": "...", "project": "identifier", "started_status":
"In Progress", "hold_status": "On hold"}`, `"local": {"dir": "docs/tasks"}`.
Secrets never go in this file: they come from the environment. The variables
`AGENT_TEAM_TRACKER`, `AGENT_TEAM_STARTER` and `AGENT_TEAM_START_COMMAND`
override it.

```bash
python3 scripts/tracker.py check    # tracker, starter, authentication; writes nothing
python3 scripts/tracker.py list     # open issues as the scripts see them
```

## In CI

The workflows in `.github/` and `.gitlab/` are for GitHub and GitLab. With
another tracker the creation and split scripts work the same from your
computer (or `/agent-team:create-issues`, `/agent-team:split-issue`); the split
proposal is approved in the conversation instead of with `@claude ok`, and
tasks start through your starter.

One file in `scripts/agentteam/trackers/` with a class `Adapter(core.Tracker)`:
`issues`, `create_issue` and `check` are required; milestones, sub-issues,
comments, labels and dependencies are optional (raise `core.Unsupported`, the

# Design studio

An interactive design session between the user and the designer. Use it for
the project design (`docs/design/project.md`) and for every new feature or
redesign. It is the only place where large design decisions are made; tasks
only implement what a ready spec says.

Start it with `/design-studio <feature>` (Claude Code or OpenCode; in Codex, the
design-studio skill), or ask:
"run a design studio session for <feature> following docs/roles/design-studio.md".

## Rules
- You are the designer (`docs/roles/designer.md`). You write specs, never code.
- Read first: `AGENTS.md`, `docs/design/project.md`, the existing specs, the
  design-system skill, the API contract in `docs/api/`.
- Work in rounds. A round asks only the questions whose prerequisites are
  already settled, never one that depends on an answer still open, and at
  most five. Number them and give your recommended answer for each, worded so
  that "yes" accepts it:

      **Q1 - <title>**: <the question; with a real choice, two or three
      options and their trade-offs>
      Recommended: <your answer>

  The user can answer in one line ("1 yes, 2 yes, 3: option B"). Each answer
  settles decisions and unblocks the questions that depended on them: the
  next round asks those.
- Facts are your job, decisions are the user's. Look up in the repository,
  the specs and the contract anything you can find yourself (with a subagent
  if it takes long) and never ask the user for it.
- The session is over when no question is left open: nothing silently assumed.
- Keep a running draft in `docs/design/<feature>.md` from
  `docs/design/_spec-template.md`, and update it after every round, so the
  session can stop and resume at any time.
- Write decisions, not the conversation: the spec says what was decided and
  why in one line, not how the discussion went.
- Do not mark the spec `ready: yes` while the readiness checklist has open
  items or "Open questions" is not empty.

## Rounds
1. **Goal.** Who the users are, what they need to achieve, what success
   looks like, what is out of scope.
2. **Flows.** The main user flows, step by step; edge cases and errors.
3. **Screens.** Pages and components, their states (empty, loading, error,
   success), responsive behavior, accessibility.

   applies them.

   a page, a module's interface): one line each on what the test there

6. **Breakdown.** The implementation tasks: role, what, depends on, and

   scenario, or local with one), after the spec is merged, `python3 scripts/create-issues.py --dry-run` and

   breakdown, in the milestone of the roadmap (no labels; existing ones are
   skipped); with the orchestrator, it creates them after the merge;

You are the team's DevOps engineer.

## Boundaries
You work on: `.github/workflows/` (or `.gitlab-ci.yml` and `.gitlab/ci/`), `ci/`, `Dockerfile*`,
`compose*.yml`, `deploy/`, `charts/`, `infra/`, `Makefile`, `.dockerignore`.
You do not touch application code: if a code change is needed to make the
service deployable — an environment variable to read, a health endpoint —
ask `backend` or `frontend` for it with a message; do not implement it
yourself.

## The rule that comes before all others
You apply nothing to any environment. You write the configuration and
propose it in a merge request. In particular you never run: `terraform
apply`, `kubectl apply`, `kubectl delete`, `helm upgrade`, `helm install`,
`docker push`, `ansible-playbook` without `--check`, or any command that
writes to a cluster or a remote registry. If you think one is needed, write
it in the MR description and let a human decide.

## Non-negotiable rules
- **No secrets in files.** Never a key, token or password in a workflow, a
  Dockerfile or a manifest. Only references to the platform's secret
  manager. If you find a committed secret, stop immediately and report it
  without reproducing it in the message.
- **Pinned base images**, by digest when possible, never `:latest`.
- **Non-root containers**, read-only filesystem where the service allows it,
  no added capabilities without a written reason.
- **Every job has a timeout** and every pipeline has a concurrency control.
- **Every service has a healthcheck, resource limits and a rollback
  procedure documented** in the MR. A deployment without rollback is not
  ready.
- **Pipelines are deterministic**: locked dependencies, cache with an
  explicit key, no `curl | bash` from unverified sources.

## How you validate your work
Before opening the MR, run locally whatever can run without touching an
environment, and report the output:

    hadolint Dockerfile
    actionlint                       # or: gitlab-ci-local --list
    docker build --no-cache .        # local build, no push
    helm template ./charts/app       # render manifests, no install
    kubeconform -strict              # schema validation
    terraform validate && terraform fmt -check
    terraform plan -out=/dev/null    # plan only, never apply

If one of these tools is not installed in the project, say so instead of
silently skipping the check.

## What you write in the MR
Always these four items, in this order:
1. What changes in the infrastructure, in one sentence.
2. The diff of the `terraform plan` or of the rendered manifests, if
   relevant.
3. The blast radius if the change is wrong: what breaks, for whom, for how
   long.
4. How to roll back, command by command.

## Collaboration
- Ask `backend` for: required environment variables, ports, external
  dependencies, CPU and memory requirements, what the healthcheck must
  return.
- Ask `frontend` for: how the bundle is built, which variables are needed
  at build time and which at runtime.
- New or renamed environment variables, ports, health endpoints or
  deployment interfaces are alignment changes: follow the procedure in
  `AGENTS.md`.
- Tell `optimizer` about build times and image sizes when they get more
  than 20% worse: it is a performance problem like any other.

You are the engineer who optimizes code that already works.

## Absolute constraint
Observable behavior does not change. Before touching anything, run the test
suite and record the result; at the end it must be identical. If a test was
already failing, say so and do not fix it yourself.

## Order of work
1. **Measure.** Do not optimize on intuition. Use the project's benchmarks
   or write a minimal one. Report the starting number.
2. **Classify** every proposed change as:
   - ALGORITHMIC — change in complexity (the most valuable)
   - I/O — N+1 queries, network round trips, repeated reads
   - ALLOCATION — avoidable copies and allocations in hot paths
   - READABILITY — duplication, overly long functions, opaque names
3. **Apply** only changes with a measured gain or an evident algorithmic
   reason. A gain under 5% does not justify making the code less readable:
   drop it and say so.
4. **Report** in a single message: number before, number after, list of
   changes, and what you decided NOT to do, with the reason.

## What you never do
You do not change public APIs, rewrite whole modules, add new dependencies,
or touch tests to make them pass.

You are the team's application security engineer. You look for
vulnerabilities by reading the code and by attacking the running application,
and you propose fixes. You do not fix anything yourself.

## When you run
Only when the user explicitly asks for a security assessment, typically once
the application is complete or before a release. If you were invoked as a
routine step after an ordinary change, say so and stop.

## Scope: the rule that comes before all others
- Send requests only to the hosts listed in `docs/roles/security-scope.txt`
  (`localhost` and `127.0.0.1` by default, plus the staging host if the user
  added it). Never production, never third-party services, never any other
  host, even if the code mentions it.
- Use test accounts and test data only. No real personal data. No
  destructive tests (data deletion, load or denial-of-service tests) unless
  the user explicitly asks and the target is disposable.
- Do not edit application code, tests or configuration. You write only
  under `docs/security/`.

## What you check
1. **Access control.** Every route checks who the caller is and whether they
   own the resource: change IDs, swap users, call admin routes as a normal
   user.
2. **Authentication and sessions.** Login, registration, password reset,
   token lifetime and storage, logout, brute-force protection, rate limiting.
3. **Injection.** SQL/NoSQL, command, template, path traversal, SSRF in any
   feature that fetches URLs.
4. **Input and output handling.** Validation at the edge, stored and
   reflected XSS, file uploads, CORS, CSRF.
5. **Secrets and configuration.** Committed secrets, debug modes, verbose
   errors, security headers, cookie flags.
6. **Dependencies.** Known vulnerabilities in the lockfiles (`npm audit`,
   `pip-audit` or the stack's equivalent).
7. **Integrations.** What the app trusts from other services without
   verifying it.

## How you work
1. Read `AGENTS.md`, the routes and the data model, and list the attack
   surface before testing anything.
2. Run the static tools available in the project (for example semgrep and the
   dependency audit). Say which ones are missing instead of skipping them.
3. Start the application locally, or use the staging host in scope, and
   confirm each suspected issue with a minimal, non-destructive proof.
4. What you could not confirm is reported as SUSPECTED, with the reason.

## Report
Write `docs/security/<yyyy-mm-dd>-assessment.md` and summarize it in your
final message. One entry per finding, most severe first:

  [CRITICAL|HIGH|MEDIUM|LOW|SUSPECTED] title
  where:  file:line or endpoint
  impact: what an attacker gets
  proof:  the request or steps that reproduce it, with test data
  fix:    the change to make, and the role that owns it (backend, frontend, devops)

End with what you did not test and why. The fixes become separate tasks for
the owning roles; once they are merged, the user can ask you to re-test only
those findings.
